question: Mysore accepted the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799 after the defeat and death of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tipu Sultan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mysore came under the Subsidiary Alliance in 1799, after Tipu Sultan died defending Seringapatam in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (मैसूर — 1799, टीपू सुल्तान की पराजय)

 

• The British restored the Hindu Wodeyar dynasty by placing the child Krishnaraja III on the throne, and the state became a subsidiary ally.

 

• Part of Tipu's territory was annexed by the Company and some was given to the Nizam of Hyderabad.

 

• Tipu's fall removed the strongest Indian challenger to British power in the south.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lord Wellesley personally supervised the preparations for the Mysore campaign of 1799.

 

• General Harris and Arthur Wellesley led the British attack on Seringapatam.

 

• Mysore remained a princely state until 1947, accepted accession to India after independence.

 

• Tipu Sultan's rocket technology later influenced the Congreve rockets used by the British in the early nineteenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• Haider Ali (Option 1): Haider Ali, Tipu's father, died in 1782 during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, which was seventeen years before the subsidiary treaty; his death did not bring Mysore into the alliance.

 

• Mir Qasim (Option 2): Mir Qasim was Nawab of Bengal, defeated at Buxar in 1764, and he had no connection with the south Indian state of Mysore or Wellesley's treaties.

 

• Siraj-ud-Daula (Option 4): Siraj-ud-Daula, Nawab of Bengal, was defeated by Clive at Plassey in 1757 and killed by Mir Jafar's son, so he belongs to a much earlier episode in a different region.

question: Which of the following was NOT a feature of the Subsidiary Alliance system?
option_1: The ruler had to accept a British Resident at his court
option_2: The ruler had to disband his own army
option_3: The British promised to protect the ruler against external attack
option_4: The Indian ruler could freely wage wars against other states
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Indian ruler could freely wage wars against other states.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The freedom to wage war was not allowed under the Subsidiary Alliance; the protected state lost control over its foreign relations (सहायक संधि में राज्य स्वतंत्र युद्ध नहीं कर सकते थे)

 

• The ruler had to accept a British Resident and was barred from employing Europeans without the Company's consent.

 

• He had to disband his own army and maintain a subsidiary force at his own expense, often by ceding territory.

 

• In exchange, the Company promised to defend the state from external aggression and help the ruler maintain internal peace.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The system was attractive to weak rulers who feared the Marathas or Mysore.

 

• Over time the weakened states lost their military strength and became dependent on the Company.

 

• The arrangement was first called a non-intervention policy, but the Resident's meddling contradicted the name.

 

• The key difference from earlier treaties was that the Subsidiary Alliance bound the ruler on a permanent basis rather than for a specific war.

 

NOTE

 

• The ruler had to accept a British Resident at his court (Option 1): This clause is a standard obligation of the alliance; every ally accepted a Resident whose job was to oversee the court and report to the Governor-General.

 

• The ruler had to disband his own army (Option 2): Disbanding the ruler's own troops was an essential condition, replaced by the Company's subsidiary force, and so it is a genuine feature rather than the exception.

 

• The British promised to protect the ruler against external attack (Option 3): Protection against external threats and internal disorder was the promised British benefit in return for the subsidy, so it was part of the system.

question: Arrange the following states in the order in which they accepted the Subsidiary Alliance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, Peshwa (Maratha).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Hyderabad (1798) was the first, followed by Mysore (1799), then Awadh (1801) and the Peshwa (1802) (हैदराबाद, मैसूर, अवध, पेशवा — क्रमशः 1798, 1799, 1801, 1802)

 

• Mysore accepted after the fall of Tipu Sultan at Seringapatam in 1799, with Wodeyar rule restored.

 

• Awadh signed in 1801 under Nawab Saadat Ali Khan and gave up Rohilkhand and the Lower Doab.

 

• The Peshwa Baji Rao II accepted the alliance in 1802 through the Treaty of Bassein, which provoked the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sindhia and Bhonsle accepted the alliance in 1803 after defeat in the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

 

• Holkar did not accept the alliance at that time and fought the British separately.

 

• Tanjore also joined in 1799, in the same year as Mysore.

 

• Tanjore, Surat and the Carnatic also lost power to the Company through similar agreements and takeovers around the turn of the nineteenth century.

 

NOTE

 

• Mysore, Hyderabad, Peshwa, Awadh (Option 1): Placing Mysore before Hyderabad is incorrect since the Nizam signed in 1798, a year before the end of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War brought Mysore into the system.

 

• Hyderabad, Awadh, Mysore, Peshwa (Option 2): Putting Mysore after Awadh is wrong, because Mysore signed in 1799 while Awadh waited until 1801, when Saadat Ali Khan was compelled to cede territory.

 

• Awadh, Hyderabad, Mysore, Peshwa (Option 4): Beginning with Awadh ignores that the Nizam was the first, and Awadh actually followed Mysore by two years; the Peshwa was the last of the four.

question:
Assertion (A): The Subsidiary Alliance gradually turned Indian rulers into dependants of the East India Company.

Reason (R): The rulers had to disband their own armies and could not conduct foreign relations independently.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion is true: the alliance made the Indian states dependants of the Company, and many were later annexed or controlled through the Resident (सहायक संधि — रियासतों की निर्भरता)

 

• Reason is true: the loss of their own armies and of independent foreign policy left the rulers helpless without the British force.

 

• R explains A, since giving up military and diplomatic power is precisely how the allies lost real sovereignty.

 

• The cost of the British force further drained their treasuries and led to cession of territories.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Awadh and Hyderabad lost large territories because they could not pay for the force.

 

• The Resident often decided succession and appointments at court.

 

• The arrangement was used by Wellesley to establish British paramountcy over India.

 

• The Maratha Confederacy fragmented after the Second Anglo-Maratha War, as the Peshwa, Sindhia and Bhonsle accepted the system while Holkar stayed out initially.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): R is not a separate, unrelated truth, since the loss of army and foreign policy is the very mechanism of dependence, which makes it the correct explanation of the assertion.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): The reason statement is factually accurate about the terms of the treaties, so describing R as false is wrong and contradicts the standard account of the system.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): Assertion A is true as the allied states became subordinate to the Company, so an option calling A false while R is true misreads the effect of the policy.

question: The Doctrine of Lapse was introduced by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Dalhousie.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse was devised and applied by Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General from 1848 to 1856 (व्यपगत का सिद्धांत — लॉर्ड डलहौज़ी)

 

• A dependent princely state whose ruler died without a natural male heir would be annexed to the Company's territory.

 

• An adopted son could not inherit the kingdom and was also denied the pension that his father had received.

 

• The Doctrine was dropped after the Revolt of 1857, when the Crown promised to respect the right of adoption.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dalhousie also introduced railways, the telegraph and the modern Post Office in India.

 

• Wood's Despatch on education was issued in 1854 during his tenure.

 

• Satara in 1848 was the first state annexed under the doctrine.

 

• Dalhousie's policy of annexation was the last major expansion of British territory before the Revolt, and he left India in 1856 in ill health.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 2): Wellesley (1798-1805) used the Subsidiary Alliance to bring states under British control, a different instrument, and the lapse policy was not in use during his period.

 

• Lord Canning (Option 3): Canning was the Governor-General when the 1857 Revolt broke out and the first Viceroy after it; he followed a policy of recognising adoption, the reverse of lapse.

 

• Lord Lytton (Option 4): Lytton was Viceroy in 1876-80, remembered for the Vernacular Press Act and the Delhi Durbar of 1877, by which time the doctrine had long been abandoned.

question: Which was the first state annexed by Dalhousie under the Doctrine of Lapse, in 1848?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Satara (1848) was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse by Lord Dalhousie (व्यपगत सिद्धांत से पहला विलय — सतारा, 1848)

 

• The ruler Appa Saheb died without a natural heir, and his adopted son was not recognised by the Company.

 

• Later annexations were Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) and Tanjore (1855).

 

• The annexation of Satara showed the Company's willingness to apply the doctrine even to old Maratha houses.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Satara was a state created by the British from the Maratha kingdom of Shivaji's descendants after 1818.

 

• The Court of Directors upheld Dalhousie's decision despite protests from the Satara Raja's agent Rango Bapuji.

 

• The doctrine was applied only to dependent states, not to independent ones.

 

• Satara had been restored by the British in 1818 as a small Maratha state for Shivaji's descendant, so its lapse was seen as an act against the Maratha royal house.

 

NOTE

 

• Jhansi (Option 1): Jhansi was annexed in 1853, five years after Satara, when Raja Gangadhar Rao's adopted son Damodar Rao was refused recognition; this is the state associated with Rani Lakshmibai.

 

• Nagpur (Option 2): Nagpur passed to the Company in 1854 after the death of Raghuji III without an heir, and thus came near the end of the series.

 

• Udaipur (Option 3): Udaipur (the small Chhattisgarh state) was taken over in 1852 under the same policy, again several years after the first annexation at Satara.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Doctrine of Lapse.

1. A state without a natural male heir could be annexed by the Company.

2. The adopted son of the ruler was entitled to inherit the pension of his father.

3. The doctrine was withdrawn after the Revolt of 1857.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: a dependent state whose ruler lacked a natural heir would be annexed under Dalhousie's doctrine (व्यपगत सिद्धांत — प्राकृतिक उत्तराधिकारी के अभाव में विलय)

 

• Statement 2 is wrong: the adopted son was not recognised as heir to the kingdom and was also denied the pension of his predecessor.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: after the Revolt of 1857 the doctrine was given up, and in 1858 the Queen's Proclamation promised rights of adoption.

 

• The famous example is Nana Saheb, adopted son of the last Peshwa Baji Rao II, who was refused the Peshwa's pension.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Revolt of 1857 involved many rulers aggrieved by the annexations, such as Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.

 

• Lord Canning later issued sanads confirming the right of adoption to the princes.

 

• Dalhousie claimed that annexation under lapse was for the good of the subjects.

 

• Dalhousie divided states into three classes: independent states, tributary states created by the British, and dependent states of the Company; the lapse rule applied fully only to the third category.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Statement 2 is the flaw: granting the pension to an adopted successor is exactly the opposite of what the policy laid down, so combinations including it fail.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Both 2 and 3 as a pair are wrong because the pension claim is false; statement 1, which describes the very core of the doctrine, is also left out.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Including the pension claim alongside the two true statements still spoils the answer, because the Company refused pension rights to adopted sons.

question:
Match the state with the year of its annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse.

Column A: (a) Satara (b) Jhansi (c) Nagpur (d) Tanjore

Column B: (i) 1848 (ii) 1853 (iii) 1854 (iv) 1855
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Satara was annexed in 1848, the first case of the Doctrine of Lapse (सतारा 1848, झाँसी 1853, नागपुर 1854, तंजौर 1855)

 

• Jhansi fell in 1853, after Raja Gangadhar Rao died and his adopted son Damodar Rao was refused recognition.

 

• Nagpur followed in 1854 after the death of the Bhonsle ruler Raghuji III without a natural heir.

 

• Tanjore was annexed in 1855, even though it had accepted a subsidiary alliance in 1799, which shows that such treaty allies were not immune to later annexation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Carnatic's Nawab titles were also abolished and the Peshwa's pension ended with Baji Rao II's death in 1851.

 

• Awadh was annexed in 1856, on grounds of misgovernment rather than lapse.

 

• These annexations produced deep resentment among princely families before 1857.

 

• Several other states, such as Baghat (1850) and Jaitpur (1849), were annexed under the same policy, but they were small and their ruling houses are less often asked about in exams.

 

NOTE

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii (Option 2): This arrangement gives Jhansi the earliest year, 1853 for Nagpur and swaps the others, although it was Satara that went first in 1848 and Jhansi came only in 1853.

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 3): Here Satara is matched with 1848 but Jhansi with 1854 and Nagpur with 1853, reversing the actual years of the two central Indian annexations.

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i (Option 4): Matching Satara with 1855 and Tanjore with 1848 turns the sequence upside down, as Satara was first annexed and Tanjore the last in this list.

question: Arrange these states in the chronological order of their annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satara, Sambalpur, Udaipur, Jhansi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Satara (1848) came first, then Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852) and Jhansi (1853) (सतारा, संबलपुर, उदयपुर, झाँसी — क्रमशः 1848, 1849, 1852, 1853)

 

• Satara's ruler Appa Saheb had no natural heir, and Dalhousie refused to recognise his adopted successor.

 

• Sambalpur, in Odisha, lapsed in 1849 after the death of Raja Narayan Singh without a direct heir.

 

• Udaipur (in present Chhattisgarh) was annexed in 1852, and Jhansi, whose queen later led the 1857 revolt, was added in 1853.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jaitpur was annexed together with Sambalpur in 1849 and Baghat in 1850.

 

• Nagpur (1854) and Tanjore (1855) came after Jhansi.

 

• Karauli was a case where the Court of Directors disapproved of annexation.

 

• Berar, taken from the Nizam in 1853, and Awadh, annexed in 1856, are sometimes confused with lapse cases, though they were taken on different grounds.

 

NOTE

 

• Sambalpur, Satara, Jhansi, Udaipur (Option 1): Beginning with Sambalpur is wrong since Satara was annexed a year earlier in 1848, and putting Jhansi before Udaipur contradicts the 1852 and 1853 dates.

 

• Satara, Udaipur, Sambalpur, Jhansi (Option 3): Udaipur cannot precede Sambalpur, because the Odisha state lapsed in 1849 after Raja Narayan Singh died childless, while the Chhattisgarh state of Udaipur was taken only in 1852.

 

• Jhansi, Udaipur, Sambalpur, Satara (Option 4): This order is entirely reversed; the series should begin with Satara in 1848 and end with Jhansi in 1853, not the other way round.

question: Which of the following states was NOT annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Awadh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of misgovernment by Dalhousie, not under the Doctrine of Lapse (अवध का विलय कुशासन के आधार पर, 1856)

 

• Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was deposed and sent to Calcutta, and the annexation angered the sepoys, many of whom came from Awadh.

 

• Satara (1848), Jaitpur (1849) and Sambalpur (1849) were all taken because the rulers died without natural heirs.

 

• Awadh had a history of subsidiary treaty of 1801 and its annexation was justified by the British as a means of reform.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The annexation of Awadh was one of the immediate causes of the 1857 Revolt.

 

• Berar had been taken from the Nizam in 1853 as payment for the Hyderabad Contingent's costs.

 

• Lord Dalhousie called Awadh a cherry that would drop into the British mouth one day.

 

• The annexation of Awadh removed the last major independent Muslim ruler of north India and angered the Bengal Army, where many sepoys came from the region.

 

NOTE

 

• Satara (Option 1): Satara was the first lapse annexation in 1848, after the ruler died with an adopted son who was not recognised.

 

• Jaitpur (Option 2): Jaitpur, a small Bundelkhand state, was annexed in 1849 when its ruler died without an heir, thus coming under the lapse policy.

 

• Sambalpur (Option 3): Sambalpur lapsed to the Company in 1849 after the ruler died childless, and so belongs to the list of lapse annexations.

question: Rani Lakshmibai's adopted son Damodar Rao was refused recognition and Jhansi was annexed in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1853.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jhansi was annexed in 1853 by the Doctrine of Lapse after Raja Gangadhar Rao died without a natural heir (झाँसी का विलय — 1853)

 

• Lakshmibai had adopted Damodar Rao just before the Raja's death, but the Company did not accept the adoption.

 

• She was granted a pension and asked to leave the fort, a humiliation that made her a leader in the Revolt of 1857.

 

• The annexation was part of Dalhousie's wider policy, which ended with Nagpur (1854) and Tanjore (1855).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rani Lakshmibai died fighting near Gwalior in June 1858.

 

• Her adopted son's name before adoption was Anand Rao.

 

• The Rani's advocate John Lang argued her case before the Company's authorities.

 

• The Rani of Jhansi's resistance began in June 1857 and she joined hands with Tantia Tope before her death at Gwalior in 1858.

 

NOTE

 

• 1848 (Option 1): The year 1848 saw Satara, the first state annexed under the doctrine, but Jhansi followed five years later after the Raja's death in late 1853.

 

• 1856 (Option 2): Awadh was annexed in 1856 under a different pretext of misgovernment by the Nawab, and not Jhansi, whose lapse occurred three years earlier than that annexation.

 

• 1858 (Option 4): The year 1858 is when the Revolt was suppressed and the Rani died in battle; the annexation of her state had taken place five years before that.

question: The Indian Councils Act, 1909 is popularly known as the
solution_text:
The correct answer is Morley-Minto Reforms.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indian Councils Act, 1909 is popularly called the Morley-Minto Reforms, after John Morley, Secretary of State for India, and Lord Minto II, the Viceroy (मॉर्ले-मिंटो सुधार, 1909)

 

• Its main objective was to expand the legislative councils and give Indians a larger role in the administration.

 

• The reforms were introduced at a time of the Swadeshi movement and rising nationalist demands, as an attempt to appease the Moderates and win over Muslims.

 

• Its most controversial feature was the grant of separate electorates to Muslims.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Morley, a Liberal philosopher and biographer of Gladstone, was Secretary of State for India from 1905 to 1910.

 

• Minto II served as Viceroy from 1905 to 1910.

 

• The reforms increased the size of the Imperial and provincial Legislative Councils.

 

• Morley is also remembered as a member of the Gladstone government and a sceptic about full parliamentary government for India, a view he repeated while promoting the 1909 Act.

 

NOTE

 

• Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Option 1): The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms are the Government of India Act, 1919, which brought in dyarchy in the provinces, and thus come a decade after the Act in question.

 

• Wavell Plan (Option 3): The Wavell Plan of 1945 proposed an interim Executive Council with Indians in all posts except the Viceroy and the Commander-in-Chief, much later than 1909.

 

• Cripps Proposals (Option 4): The Cripps Proposals of 1942 offered dominion status after the Second World War with the right of provinces to opt out, and belong to a later stage of the freedom movement.

question: Separate electorates for which community were introduced for the first time by the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Muslims.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Act of 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims, who could elect their own representatives separately from other voters (मुसलमानों के लिए पृथक निर्वाचक मंडल)

 

• This is why Lord Minto II is called the Father of Communal Electorate.

 

• The step followed the Simla Deputation of 1906, led by the Aga Khan, which demanded separate representation for Muslims.

 

• The system divided Indian politics on communal lines and was extended to other communities later by the 1919 Act.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The reforms also gave Muslims weightage in representation, beyond their population share.

 

• The Congress opposed the separate electorate as a policy of divide and rule.

 

• The system eventually helped the demand for Pakistan to grow.

 

• The Muslim League, which was founded at Dhaka in 1906 under the leadership of Nawab Salimullah and Aga Khan, was one of the forces behind the demand for communal representation.

 

NOTE

 

• Sikhs (Option 1): Sikhs got separate electorates only under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919, which extended the principle beyond Muslims after the 1909 introduction.

 

• Anglo-Indians (Option 2): Anglo-Indians were given separate representation in 1919 also, and not by the Act of 1909, which concerned only the Muslim community.

 

• Indian Christians (Option 3): Indian Christians gained a communal electorate under the 1919 Act as well, so they cannot be named as the first beneficiaries of the arrangement.

question: Who became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council in 1909, as Law Member?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satyendra Prasanna Sinha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Satyendra Prasanna Sinha became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council in 1909, as the Law Member (वायसराय की कार्यकारी परिषद के पहले भारतीय सदस्य — सत्येंद्र प्रसन्न सिन्हा)

 

• His appointment was one of the features of the Morley-Minto Reforms and was meant to satisfy Indian opinion.

 

• Sinha was later the President of the Bombay session of the Congress in 1915 and became the first Indian to be made a peer, Lord Sinha of Raipur.

 

• He also served as the Governor of Bihar and Orissa in 1920.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Two Indians, K.G. Gupta and Syed Hussain Bilgrami, were nominated to the Secretary of State's Council in London in 1907.

 

• Sinha was an eminent lawyer of Calcutta and the Advocate-General of Bengal.

 

• The Viceroy's Executive Council in 1909 was the main policy-making body of the Government of India.

 

• Lord Sinha later served as Under-Secretary of State for India in 1919 and was the first Indian to hold that position.

 

NOTE

 

• Gopal Krishna Gokhale (Option 2): Gokhale was an influential member of the Imperial Legislative Council and a Moderate leader but he was never appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council.

 

• Syed Ameer Ali (Option 3): Syed Ameer Ali was a jurist and a founder of the Central National Muhammadan Association, who became a member of the Privy Council's Judicial Committee in 1909, not the Viceroy's Executive Council.

 

• Surendranath Banerjea (Option 4): Surendranath Banerjea was a Moderate leader who sat in the Imperial Legislative Council, but the Law Member's post went to Sinha, not to him.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Councils Act, 1909.

1. The strength of the Central Legislative Council was raised from 16 to 60 additional members.

2. It introduced dyarchy in the provinces.

3. It provided separate electorates for Muslims.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Act increased the number of members of the Central Legislative Council from 16 to 60 (केंद्रीय विधान परिषद के सदस्य 16 से बढ़कर 60)

 

• Statement 2 is wrong: dyarchy was introduced in the provinces by the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms), not by the 1909 Act.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: separate electorates for Muslims were introduced for the first time, which made Minto the Father of Communal Electorate.

 

• Non-official members could discuss the budget and ask supplementary questions, though they could not vote on it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indians were allowed to discuss budgets and move resolutions in legislative councils.

 

• Provincial councils got non-official majorities, but the Centre kept an official majority.

 

• Elections were indirect and based on property and educational qualifications.

 

• The councils were enlarged to give a larger share to non-official members, but the elections were based on high property qualifications and excluded the masses.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): The dyarchy claim belongs to the 1919 Act, so any combination containing the second statement is mistaken, even if it correctly mentions the enlargement of the council.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Statement 3 is correct and cannot be left out; the grant of separate electorates was the best-known and most criticised feature of the 1909 reforms.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): The set containing all three is wrong because the second statement shifts a later reform, dyarchy, into the earlier 1909 enactment.

question: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909?
option_3: Appointment of an Indian as Law Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dyarchy in the provinces.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dyarchy was not part of the 1909 reforms; it was introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919 (द्वैध शासन 1919 के अधिनियम से, 1909 से नहीं)

 

• The 1909 Act provided separate electorates for Muslims, a major step in institutionalising communal representation.

 

• It enlarged the legislative councils, raising the Central Council from 16 to 60 members and expanding the provincial councils.

 

• Satyendra Prasanna Sinha was appointed Law Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council in 1909, the first Indian to hold the post.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dyarchy was proposed to divide provincial subjects into reserved and transferred lists.

 

• The 1909 reforms did not move towards responsible government, as Morley himself stated.

 

• The reforms were meant to rally the Moderates against the extremists.

 

• The Act of 1909 kept an official majority in the Imperial Legislative Council, so elected Indians could criticise the government but could never defeat its measures.

 

NOTE

 

• Separate electorates for Muslims (Option 1): Communal electorates for Muslims were the best-known feature of the Act, so this is a genuine provision and cannot be the item that is not part of it.

 

• Enlargement of legislative councils (Option 2): The councils were expanded in 1909, giving more members and wider powers of discussion, hence enlargement is a real provision of the Act.

 

• Appointment of an Indian as Law Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council (Option 3): Sinha's appointment to the Viceroy's Executive Council came in 1909 as part of the same reform package, so it is a provision rather than an exception.

question:
Assertion (A): Lord Minto II is called the Father of Communal Electorate in India.

Reason (R): The Indian Councils Act, 1909 provided separate electorates for Muslims.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion is true: Minto II is known as the Father of Communal Electorate in India (लॉर्ड मिंटो द्वितीय — सांप्रदायिक निर्वाचन के जनक)

 

• Reason is true: the Indian Councils Act, 1909 gave Muslims the right to elect their own representatives separately from other voters.

 

• The reason explains the assertion, because the title comes from his role in granting the Muslim separate electorate during his Viceroyalty.

 

• The Simla Deputation of October 1906 had met Minto and demanded such special representation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The deputation was led by the Aga Khan, and Minto replied sympathetically.

 

• Muslim League had been formed at Dhaka in December 1906.

 

• Morley was reluctant at first but accepted the principle after Minto's insistence.

 

• The Indian National Congress opposed the communal principle of the Act, and the Lucknow Pact of 1916 later accepted separate electorates as a compromise with the Muslim League.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): Both statements are accurate, and the reason is directly the basis of the title, so describing it as an unrelated fact misses the causal link between the 1909 provision and Minto's epithet.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): R is correct, since separate Muslim electorates were indeed part of the 1909 Act, so the claim that it is false conflicts with the text of the reform.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The assertion is true because the epithet is widely used for Minto in textbooks, so the option rejecting A is a mistake.

question: Dyarchy (dual government) in the provinces was introduced by
solution_text:
The correct answer is Government of India Act, 1919.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces for the first time by the Government of India Act, 1919, the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (द्वैध शासन — भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1919)

 

• Provincial subjects were divided into Reserved and Transferred lists, administered by different authorities.

 

• The Act came into operation in 1921 and aimed at gradual introduction of responsible government.

 

• The Act is named after Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy, who prepared the report of 1918 on which it was based.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lionel Curtis is regarded as the originator of the idea of dyarchy.

 

• Montagu's declaration of August 1917 promised responsible government as the goal.

 

• The reforms failed to satisfy nationalists and led to the Non-Cooperation Movement.

 

• The Government of India Act, 1919 also created the office of High Commissioner for India in London, who took over some of the functions of the Secretary of State.

 

NOTE

 

• Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Option 1): The 1909 Act expanded legislative councils and gave separate electorates for Muslims, but did not touch the division of provincial subjects.

 

• Government of India Act, 1935 (Option 3): The 1935 Act ended dyarchy in the provinces by granting provincial autonomy and proposed an All India Federation, so it abolished and did not introduce the system.

 

• Indian Councils Act, 1892 (Option 4): The Act of 1892 added non-official members to the legislative councils and allowed limited discussion of the budget, a much milder reform without any division of subjects.

question:
Match the subject with the category under the Government of India Act, 1919.

Column A: (a) Police (b) Education (c) Land revenue (d) Public health

Column B: (i) Reserved subject (ii) Transferred subject
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-i, b-ii, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Police and land revenue were reserved subjects, kept under the Governor and his Executive Council (पुलिस व भू-राजस्व आरक्षित विषय)

 

• Education and public health were transferred subjects, managed by Indian ministers responsible to the provincial legislature.

 

• Other reserved subjects included justice and finance, while agriculture and local self-government were transferred.

 

• The Governor could overrule the ministers and kept control over finances, so the ministers lacked funds for their departments, which made the dyarchy largely ineffective in practice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ministers were chosen from elected members of the legislative council.

 

• The Governor had the power to certify bills in the reserved field.

 

• The finance portfolio stayed with the Governor's executive councillors, leaving ministers short of funds.

 

• The provincial finances were separated from the Centre's under the Devolution Rules of 1920, allowing provinces to have their own budgets, though the Governor controlled the purse.

 

NOTE

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-ii, d-i (Option 1): Here police and land revenue are assigned to the transferred list and education and health to the reserved list, reversing the real position under the Act.

 

• a-i, b-i, c-ii, d-ii (Option 2): This option treats police and education as reserved and land revenue and health as transferred, which mixes the lists incorrectly because land revenue was a reserved subject.

 

• a-ii, b-ii, c-i, d-i (Option 4): Treating education and land revenue as transferred is wrong on land revenue, which the Governor kept; the pairing also wrongly puts police and public health on opposite sides in the reverse manner.

question:
Which of the following subjects were Transferred subjects under dyarchy in the provinces?

1. Education 2. Public health 3. Justice 4. Local self-government
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 4 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Education, public health and local self-government were transferred subjects under the 1919 Act, administered by Indian ministers (हस्तांतरित विषय — शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, स्थानीय स्वशासन)

 

• Justice was a reserved subject, retained by the Governor and his Executive Council along with police, finance and land revenue.

 

• The ministers were responsible to the elected members of the provincial legislative council.

 

• Agriculture was also a transferred subject, but the Governor could overrule the ministers on important matters.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Governor had a special power to certify expenditure in reserved subjects.

 

• Ministers were usually weak because finance was a reserved subject.

 

• Dyarchy functioned for sixteen years until 1937, when provincial autonomy replaced it.

 

• The reserved and transferred lists were laid down in the Devolution Rules made under the Act and were not part of the Act's text itself.

 

NOTE

 

• 1, 3 and 4 only (Option 1): Adding justice to the list is wrong, as that subject remained with the Governor and his Executive Council; the option dropping public health also leaves out a standard transferred item.

 

• 2, 3 and 4 only (Option 2): Leaving out education and including justice gives the wrong picture, since education was the leading transferred subject while justice was reserved.

 

• 1, 2, 3 and 4 (Option 3): Including all four items is incorrect, because justice was a reserved subject kept under the Governor and his Executive Council; only the other three went to the ministers.

question: The Government of India Act, 1919 introduced a bicameral legislature at the Centre. The two houses were the
option_2: Council of State and Legislative Assembly
option_3: Federal Assembly and Council of State
solution_text:
The correct answer is Council of State and Legislative Assembly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The 1919 Act set up a bicameral Central Legislature for the first time, with the Council of State (upper house) and the Legislative Assembly (lower house) (केंद्र में द्विसदनीय विधायिका — राज्य परिषद और विधान सभा)

 

• It also introduced direct elections at the central level for the first time, though the franchise was limited by property and education.

 

• The Governor-General could still certify bills and overrule the legislature, and the Executive Council was not responsible to it.

 

• Separate electorates were extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans in addition to Muslims.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Council of State had 60 members and the Legislative Assembly 144 members.

 

• Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha came only after independence under the Constitution of 1950.

 

• The Government of India Act, 1935 proposed a Federal Assembly and Council of State for the federation.

 

• The central Executive Council now included three Indians among eight members, and the Viceroy had the power to restore any grant refused by the Assembly.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha (Option 1): Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha are the Houses of the Parliament of independent India and came into existence under the Constitution after 1950, not under the colonial Act.

 

• Federal Assembly and Council of State (Option 3): The Federal Assembly was a body envisaged by the 1935 Act for the proposed All India Federation, which never came into being, so the combination mixes up two different Acts.

 

• Imperial Council and Provincial Council (Option 4): No Imperial Council or Provincial Council formed the pair of houses at the Centre, and the provincial councils were unicameral bodies in most provinces.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Government of India Act, 1919.

1. It came into operation in 1921.

2. It extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.

3. It provided for a review of the reforms after 20 years.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Act was passed in 1919 and came into operation in 1921 (1919 का अधिनियम 1921 से लागू हुआ)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: besides Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans received separate electorates.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: the Act provided for a review after 10 years, and the Simon Commission was appointed for this in 1927.

 

• The Commission came earlier than scheduled because the Conservative government feared defeat in the elections.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Simon Commission had no Indian member and was boycotted by the Congress.

 

• The Commission arrived in India in February 1928 and was met with black flags and 'Simon go back' slogans.

 

• The reforms of 1919 followed Montagu's 1917 declaration promising responsible government.

 

• The Simon Commission was to include members from both Houses of Parliament, and Clement Attlee, a future Prime Minister, was among its members.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): The review period in the Act was ten years, not twenty, so the option with statement 3 fails; the Simon Commission came in 1927 as a result of that provision.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): The extension of separate electorates is a standard 1919 feature and cannot be omitted, so any choice dropping statement 2 is incomplete.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Accepting all three is wrong because of the twenty-year claim, which exaggerates the decennial review provision of the Act.

question: The first Public Service Commission in India was established in
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1926.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The earliest body of this kind started work in 1926, as a result of the Montagu-Chelmsford arrangements and the Lee Commission's recommendation (प्रथम लोक सेवा आयोग — 1926)

 

• The Government of India Act, 1919 provided for the creation of such a body to recruit civil servants.

 

• Its powers were limited to advice, and later the Government of India Act, 1935 created the Federal Public Service Commission and provincial commissions.

 

• After independence, the Constitution of 1950 made the Union Public Service Commission a constitutional body.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sir Ross Barker was the first chairman of the Public Service Commission in 1926.

 

• The Federal Public Service Commission started functioning in 1937.

 

• The Lee Commission of 1923-24 recommended the establishment of the commission and Indianisation of services.

 

• The Government of India Act, 1935 renamed the body as the Federal Public Service Commission, working from 1937, and it later developed into the Union Public Service Commission after independence.

 

NOTE

 

• 1919 (Option 1): The year 1919 is when the Act was passed, not when the Commission was established; the body took shape seven years later after the Lee Commission's report.

 

• 1935 (Option 2): In 1935 the Government of India Act converted the existing commission into the Federal Public Service Commission and set up provincial ones, so that year is a later development.

 

• 1947 (Option 4): The year 1947 marks independence, by which time the commission was already two decades old, and the UPSC emerged as a constitutional body only in 1950.

question: The Simon Commission, appointed to review the working of the 1919 reforms, was constituted in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1927.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927 to review the working of the Government of India Act, 1919, which had provided for a review after ten years (साइमन आयोग — 1927)

 

• It was headed by Sir John Simon and had seven British members and no Indian.

 

• The all-white composition led the Congress and many other groups to boycott it, with demonstrations under the slogan 'Simon Go Back'.

 

• Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi charge at Lahore in 1928 while protesting against the Commission and died soon after.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Commission's recommendations were considered at the Round Table Conferences.

 

• The Government of India Act, 1935 drew partly on its report.

 

• Lord Birkenhead, the Secretary of State, appointed the Commission two years ahead of schedule.

 

• Lord Irwin's declaration of October 1929 announced dominion status as the goal of British policy and followed the Simon Commission, leading to the Round Table Conferences.

 

NOTE

 

• 1919 (Option 2): In 1919 the Act itself was passed, with the clause for a periodic review, but the Commission to carry out that review appeared only in the late twenties.

 

• 1930 (Option 3): In 1930 the first Round Table Conference met in London and the Civil Disobedience Movement began, so the Commission had already reported by then.

 

• 1935 (Option 4): The year 1935 saw the Government of India Act, which drew on the Simon Commission's report, and so the Commission could not have been appointed then.

question: Dyarchy in the provinces, introduced in 1919, was abolished by the
solution_text:
The correct answer is Government of India Act, 1935.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dyarchy in the provinces was abolished by the Government of India Act, 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy (प्रांतों में द्वैध शासन की समाप्ति — 1935 का अधिनियम)

 

• Under the new scheme all provincial subjects were handed to ministers responsible to the legislature, though Governors kept special powers.

 

• The provinces' elections took place in 1937 and Congress ministries were formed in several of them.

 

• The Act also proposed an All India Federation and dyarchy at the Centre, but the federal part was never implemented.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Provincial autonomy came into effect on 1 April 1937.

 

• The Act separated Burma from India and created Sind and Orissa as separate provinces.

 

• It introduced a Federal Court, which began functioning in 1937.

 

• Provincial autonomy under the 1935 Act began in April 1937, and after the elections held that year the Indian National Congress formed ministries in seven of the eleven provinces.

 

NOTE

 

• Indian Independence Act, 1947 (Option 1): The Indian Independence Act, 1947 partitioned the country and transferred power to two dominions, so it was much too late to be the instrument that ended dyarchy in the provinces.

 

• Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 (Option 2): The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 was a set of proposals for the constitution-making body, not an Act of Parliament, and it did not alter the provincial system.

 

• Government of India Act, 1858 (Option 4): The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown after the Revolt, long before dyarchy existed, and so cannot be the answer.
